metadata.title: UPGRADING THE ICT QUESTIONNAIRE ITEMS IN PISA 2021

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This document is a framework and questionnaire-development paper for PISA 2021 ICT items, not an analysis of PISA microdata with achievement outcomes. It describes a multistage development process (literature review, expert group input, qualitative cognitive-lab testing) rather than estimating model parameters from a representative student sample. As a result, there is no reported application of PISA sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife) for statistical inference. For any future empirical use of the PISA 2021 ICT questionnaire data, analysts should apply the standard PISA complex-sample weights provided in the PISA database for the relevant countries and cycles, and use replicate weights if variance estimation is required.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This paper does not conduct an empirical predictive analysis of PISA cognitive achievement outcomes using plausible values (PVs). Instead, it documents the rationale, conceptual framework, and item-upgrading process for the PISA 2021 ICT questionnaire, including cognitive-lab testing of draft items. Because there is no PV-based dependent variable and no reported statistical modeling pipeline, PV handling and missing-data handling strategies are not applicable to the study’s purpose.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The paper does not report an analytic student sample from PISA microdata. It describes qualitative cognitive-lab testing with 15-year-old students (14 interviews conducted in total, seven per language) to assess item wording, comprehension, and respondent burden; it also notes that teacher and principal ICT questionnaire drafts were desk-reviewed. For the PISA 2021 ICT questionnaire development itself, no country-level analytic sample selection criteria are provided.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD paper explains why and how the PISA 2021 ICT questionnaire was upgraded, moving from older emphases on device availability and intensity toward a framework centered on the quality of ICT resources, detailed modalities of ICT use (including learning vs leisure and in-school vs out-of-school contexts), and students’ self-reported ICT competencies and attitudes. It synthesizes lessons from previous PISA ICT questionnaire cycles and related literature, then presents the PISA 2021 ICT framework that guides item development. The development process includes expert-group guidance and qualitative cognitive-lab testing of student questionnaire items (14 one-on-one interviews across French and English), with desk review for teacher/principal items. The paper reports no ML model performance metrics and does not estimate causal or predictive effects; its contribution is instrument design and policy-relevant measurement coverage for future PISA cycles.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is a non-empirical methodology/instrument-development paper: it does not analyze a representative PISA student dataset to produce predictive or causal estimates. Consequently, fields that depend on an empirical modeling pipeline (e.g., total_students for an analytic sample, PV handling for achievement DVs, missing-data handling for model estimation, and ML techniques with performance metrics) are not populated. The paper’s evidence base is primarily conceptual (framework rationale) and qualitative (cognitive-lab testing of draft items), so the extraction focuses on survey instrument development rather than statistical results.
